title: Every Root-to-Leaf Route
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. List every route that starts at the root and ends at a leaf, a node with no children at all.

Write each route as the node values joined by "->", for example "4->9->1". Return the routes in any order.

examples.why: Three leaves (5, 1 and 0), so three routes. Node 9 has children, so it never ends a route.
The root has only a right child. The root is not a leaf, so there is no route that stops at it.
A lone root is a leaf. Negative values keep their minus sign.

hints: A route is finished exactly when you stand on a node whose left and right child are both missing.
Walk down with depth-first search and carry the route built so far as you go.
At each node append its value to the route. If it is a leaf, save the route; otherwise recurse into the children that exist, passing the extended route.

explain.intuition:
Every leaf has exactly one route from the root, so the answer has one string per leaf. A depth-first walk visits nodes in exactly the order a route grows: you go down one edge, extend the route, and when you hit a leaf the route is complete.

The only trap is the leaf test. A node with one child is not a leaf, so a route must not stop there. Checking node == null instead of "no children" produces fake routes that end at half-empty nodes.
steps: Start a DFS at the root with an empty route.
At each node, add its value to the route (with "->" if the route is not empty).
If both children are missing, push the route to the answer.
Otherwise recurse into each child that exists with the extended route.
pitfalls: Saving a route when you reach a null child. A node with one child then yields an extra, wrong route like "2" in the second example.
Building one shared array and forgetting to undo the push after returning from a child, so later routes carry values from earlier branches.
Formatting negatives oddly. "10->-20" is correct; just join the numbers as they are.

complexity.time: O(n · h), the cost of writing out the strings
complexity.space: O(h) for the recursion, plus the output

solutions.title: Recursive DFS passing the route string
solutions.idea: Pass the route built so far down the recursion. Strings are immutable, so each branch automatically gets its own copy.

solutions.title: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
solutions.idea: Push (node, list of values so far) pairs. Pop one; if it is a leaf, join its values; otherwise push its children with the extended list.

followups: Return only the routes whose values add up to a target. Where do you prune?
The tree has a million nodes and is very deep. How do you avoid a stack overflow and the O(n · h) copying cost?
